title: Old man and corruption; renew the mind; truth and anger (Eph 4:22–26)
english: sin is to be understood as meant. For by his former way of life and the desires of deceit, through sinning and never doing anything that belongs to incorruption but working everything that belongs to corruption, this man is always being corrupted. So the desires of deceit and the former way of life bring about his corruption; and as long as he does these things he has not yet been wholly corrupted, but he is being corrupted. The Word of God, however, does not corrupt: he kills the old man in order to make him alive. “For I kill,” he says, “and I make alive” (Deuteronomy 32:39); and “when he killed them, then they sought him” (Psalm 78:34).

You will ask further how the old man is the one grown old in wickedness. Perhaps, just as virtue renews and creates afresh, so wickedness, its opposite, makes old, so that signs of age, wrinkles as it were, appear on the soul, as they do on bodies growing old. That is why Christ presents the church to himself glorious, “not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27). For as long as one bears the signs of age, one has the wrinkle too; but when one puts off the old man, everything is in its prime and every wrinkle vanishes. And the desire of deceit is wicked and base desire.

“And be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23). If, by this wording, we must be renewed neither simply in the spirit nor in the mind, but in the spirit of our mind, we must ask on its own what our mind is and what its spirit is. Notice also the words “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also; I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). Consider, then, whether, just as there are many spirits and each belongs closely to someone, so there is a spirit that belongs to our mind; and when our mind is being cleansed and has thrown off all its mist, this spirit, being its own, renews us.

“And put on the new man, created according to God” (Ephesians 4:24). If we want to put on the new man created according to God, let us take to heart “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1), and “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). In a word, we will show Christ formed in us, whole, and in every action.

“Therefore, putting away the lie, speak truth each one with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4:25). Simpler readers will think that nothing more than a moral rule is said here. But we are persuaded that the lie is the opposite of the truth, and so the lie we seek to put away, the one opposed to the truth that is fittingly spoken to the neighbor alone, is false belief. It is no ordinary task to put away that lie, and to put away a lie of this kind; for one must be an approved money-changer, able to test everything, so that we hold fast only to what is good and keep away from every form of evil (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22). And what stands against the lie that lies in false beliefs is saving truth. The words “speak truth each one with his neighbor” are taken from Zechariah (Zechariah 8:16).

“Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). It is clear that this is taken from the fourth Psalm (Psalm 4:4). The word “be angry” signifies two things. One is the involuntary, which some have called a pre-passion; it will happen even to the perfect, who suffer something involuntary when circumstances of this kind provoke them to anger. The other is when assent already accepts that it is fitting to punish the one thought to have done wrong; and this, since it lies in our power, the apostle commands us to put away. So it is the first of these meanings that is shown in “Be angry and do not sin,” in place of “even if you have at some time admitted anger, leave it without effect.”

“Do not let the sun go down on your provocation” (Ephesians 4:26). If we take this as said of the sun we see, then we will sin when we are angry and keep our anger while the sun goes down, which I think is absurd.
